state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think Fido falling asleep would result in a negative-sloping section on the graph? Let me ask you this: what would happen if you tried your method on a simpler version of the problem?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, well if Fido was asleep, the line would be flat, wouldn't it? So that doesn't really make sense... But I'm confused about what the negative slope means then - does it mean he's going backwards towards his home, or something?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: If Fido was asleep, you mentioned the line would be flat. So, what does the negative slope suggest about Fido's movement on the graph? Let me ask you this: what would happen if you considered the relationship between time and distance in a different way on this graph?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if the line is going down, that means the distance is getting smaller, so Fido must be getting closer to his home... he's walking back towards it? So the negative slope means he's moving back, not that he's asleep or anything?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the rest/movement confusion by prompting the student to reason through the graph's meaning, leading to clear resolution of the misconception, though some questions are slightly redundant.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher perfectly exemplifies the Socratic method by exclusively using probing questions to guide the student's reasoning, never providing direct answers, and prompting the student to identify the flaw in their own logic about the sleeping dog.
